title: The Bobo doll study
question: Will young children copy aggression that they have only watched?
authors: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila A. Ross
citation: Bandura, A., Ross, D., & Ross, S. A. (1961). Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63(3), 575-582.
imageAlt: An illustrated reconstruction of Room 1: a child at a table with potato stamps and stickers watches a woman kneel on a large inflatable clown and punch its nose.
intro: In about 1960, at Stanford University in California, 72 children aged three to five took part in a simple experiment. Some watched an adult attack a large inflatable clown, a Bobo doll, with punches, kicks, a mallet and shouts of "Pow!". Some watched an adult play quietly. Some saw no adult at all.

A few minutes later, each child was taken to another room with a smaller Bobo doll and left to play while the experimenter did paperwork in a corner. Many of the children who had watched the aggressive adult copied the adult's exact acts and words. The other children almost never did.

The study showed that children can learn new behaviour just by watching, with no reward. It led to Bandura's social learning theory and to decades of argument about violence on screen. It is also a good case for practising critical analysis, because almost every perspective in your course reads it differently.

title: The $1 and $20 experiment
question: If you are paid to tell a lie, will you come to believe it more when the payment is small?
authors: Leon Festinger and James M. Carlsmith
citation: Festinger, L., & Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203-210.
imageAlt: An illustrated reconstruction of the key moment: in a 1950s office, a male student smiles and gestures as he tells a young woman that the experiment is fun, while she listens with a doubtful look. A tape recorder can be seen in a cabinet.
intro: In the late 1950s, at Stanford University in California, male students spent an hour doing deliberately boring tasks: putting spools on a tray and turning pegs on a board. Then the experimenter asked some of them for a favour. Would they tell the next participant, a young woman waiting outside, that the tasks were fun? Some were paid $1 for this, others $20.

Later, in what seemed to be an unrelated interview, the students rated how enjoyable the tasks had been. Students paid $1 said they had enjoyed the tasks more than students paid $20, and more than students who had not been asked to lie at all. The $20 students' ratings were close to those of students who had not been asked to lie.

The result went against common sense and against the reward-based theories of the time. It became the classic test of Leon Festinger's theory of cognitive dissonance, the idea that people change their beliefs to fit what they have done. It is also a good case for critical analysis: it relies on layers of deception, rests on a small sample of young American men, and has been explained in rival ways by almost every perspective in your course.
